title: Drupal node revisions are not business-event records, so a public-sector approval loses its actor and rule
content:
Drupal keeps node revisions: successive versions of content, each with a timestamp and the author of the edit. The research draws the distinction that matters for public administration — a revision records that text changed, whereas an approval is a decision, taken by an actor, under a rule.

These are different objects. A revision can show that a page moved from unpublished to published; it cannot express that the publication was authorised, by whom in what role, or against which requirement. Reconstructing the decision from revision history means inferring intent from field diffs, which is exactly the kind of evidence an auditor will not accept.

publicplan delivers Drupal into the public sector, so the gap appears at the point where content workflow meets administrative accountability. The addressable unit is small: the approval events already occur as user actions inside the CMS, but nothing durable is written at the moment they happen.
